chapters.title: The Elements of Behavior
chapters.keys: Stop blaming yourself and start reading behavior as a system. Fogg's Behavior Model says a behavior happens only when three things meet at the same moment: Motivation (your desire to do it), Ability (your capacity to do it), and a Prompt (the cue that says do it now). When a behavior is not happening, troubleshoot in this order: is there a prompt, is it easy enough to do, and only last, is motivation the problem. Usually the fix is a prompt or an easier version, not wanting it harder. This week, take one behavior you keep failing at and ask which of the three is missing, instead of calling yourself lazy. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.

chapters.title: Motivation: Focus on Matching
chapters.keys: Motivation is unreliable, so do not build a habit on it. It rises and falls in waves you cannot count on. Start from an aspiration, list many specific behaviors that could serve it, and sort them with Focus Mapping, rating each by how effective it would be and how much you want to do it. Pick Golden Behaviors, meaning ones that are effective, that you want to do, and that you can do. This week, run that sort on one aspiration. Reversal: when a wave of motivation does come, use it for a hard one-time task that makes the later habit easier, such as buying equipment or clearing the space, not to commit to a heroic daily routine. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.

chapters.title: Ability: Easy Does It
chapters.keys: Make it easy, because simplicity changes behavior. Ask the Discovery Question: what is making this behavior hard to do? Check the Ability Chain, the five factors of time, money, physical effort, mental effort and fit with your routine, since the weakest link decides. Then fix it in one of three ways: build skill, get a tool or resource, or shrink the behavior to a tiny version or a Starter Step (the very first move, like putting on your shoes). Story the author tells: Fogg's own flossing habit, where he committed to flossing just one tooth, the effort was so small he kept doing it, and it grew into flossing his whole mouth.

chapters.title: Prompts: The Power of After
chapters.keys: Do not rely on memory or willpower to start a habit; attach it to something you already do. Fogg calls that existing routine an Anchor and writes the habit as a recipe: after I do this anchor, I will do this tiny behavior. Pick an anchor that fits where it happens, how often it happens and what kind of habit you are adding, and place the new behavior immediately after it. Fogg names three kinds of prompt: a person prompt comes from inside you (a body signal, an urge, your own memory), a context prompt comes from the surroundings (a phone alert, a note, an object in view), and an action prompt is a behavior you just did, which is the anchor; for building habits the action prompt is the best of the three. This week, write one recipe and run it. Story the author tells: Fogg's own two push-ups after using the bathroom, which stuck because the anchor happened many times a day.

chapters.title: Emotions Create Habits
chapters.keys: Emotions create habits, not repetition. Right after you do the tiny behavior, Celebrate, meaning you deliberately make yourself feel good and successful on the spot, with a fist pump, a word or a smile. That feeling, which Fogg calls Shine, is what wires the habit in, and it connects to his second maxim: help people feel successful. Celebrate right after the behavior, not later. This week, practice one celebration that feels real to you and use it the instant you finish. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.

chapters.title: Growing Your Habits from Tiny to Transformative
chapters.keys: Start tiny and let the habit grow on its own; do not force it bigger. Habits grow in two ways: the behavior gets larger, such as more push-ups, and one habit spreads into others, because each success builds your skill and confidence at changing. This week, do the tiny version, allow yourself to do more when you feel like it, and never demand more as the new minimum. Story the author tells: Fogg's push-up habit, which grew from two at a time into many per day as he kept going.

chapters.title: Untangling Bad Habits: A Systematic Solution
chapters.keys: Do not attack a bad habit head on with willpower; untangle it in steps. Break the habit into its specific behaviors and start with the easiest. To stop a behavior, work the same three levers as for starting one, in this order: take away the prompt, make the behavior harder to do, and only last, reduce motivation. Then swap in a new behavior where the old one used to happen. If nothing has worked, scale the change back. This week, pick one specific behavior of one bad habit and take away its prompt. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.

chapters.title: How We Change Together
chapters.keys: Use the same tools with families, teams and communities that you use on yourself. Find what the other people already want, make that behavior easy for them, give it a good prompt, and help them feel successful. This week, pick one shared behavior and design for it, instead of lecturing or pushing. Reversal: these methods are for helping people do what they already want to do, not for making them do what they do not want, and Fogg treats the ethics of changing others as part of the chapter. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence; Fogg gives a family case and a hospital staff stress case, but their details are not recalled with confidence.
